questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The Académie française and what its members do
questions.learningObjective: state the founding date of the Académie and the job of its members
questions.stem: An institution founded in 1635 under the patronage of Cardinal Richelieu still works on written French, and what it says is advice rather than law. What do its members actually do?

options.text: They license publishers and decide which books may be printed in the French language
options.misconception: believes the body holds a censorship power over publishing

options.text: They teach French in state schools and set the examination papers for the baccalaureat
options.misconception: believes the body runs the school system and the examinations

options.text: They certify that a document is legally valid, in the way a notary certifies a signature
options.misconception: believes the body performs a notarial function

options.text: They work on the dictionary and on usage, and each of them is known by the name of a seat rather than a personal name

questions.explanation: The Académie was set up in 1635 by Cardinal Richelieu, and its stated task was to give the French language a settled form rather than to police speech. The work is a dictionary, a series of editions, and a continuing discussion of usage, and the forty members are addressed by the name of their chair, the fauteuil they occupy, so that a writer can cite the judgement of the seat rather than of a person. The first edition of the dictionary appeared in 1694. What the body does not do is teach, certify, or license, and its judgements bind nobody: a spelling it dislikes is a spelling a publisher may still use.
questions.hint: Ask what a dictionary committee does, and ask what a ministry of education does.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Why the first Academy dictionary took decades to appear
questions.learningObjective: connect the founding of the Académie in 1635 with the first dictionary in 1694
questions.stem: An institution was founded in 1635 and produced its first dictionary in 1694. How many years separate the two events, and what does the gap suggest?

options.text: 6 years, which suggests the institution set to work immediately and met no obstacle at all
options.misconception: reads the last two digits of each year as the interval

options.text: 69 years, which suggests the work was interrupted by a war and resumed only much later
options.misconception: adds the digits of each year instead of subtracting the years

options.text: 59 years, which suggests the dictionary was a private venture with no connection to the institution
options.misconception: computes the interval correctly and then reads the wrong cause into it

options.text: 59 years, which suggests the members judged that fixing usage needed slow comparison rather than a quick vote

questions.explanation: The interval is 1694 minus 1635, which is 59 years. The gap is the point of the question rather than an inconvenience, because an institution charged with settling a language could not do it by drafting a list in an afternoon: the work meant comparing usage across writers, arguing about which forms were genuinely current, and waiting for a form to be found acceptable rather than merely possible. A short interval would have produced a dictionary nobody used, since a list invented in a year would have recorded the preferences of forty people instead of the habits of a language.
questions.hint: Subtract the earlier year from the later one before reading anything into the result.

The two other names in the options belong to different dictionaries of a different century: Larousse is the nineteenth-century dictionary of everyday language, and Littré is the monumental dictionary built on literary usage, whose title is the surname of its editor. The fourth option tests a separate confusion, since a reader who knows Larousse as a publisher may assume it is behind every large French dictionary. Knowing which editor gave which dictionary its name is enough to place the works in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The CNRTL and what its full name promises
questions.learningObjective: read the full name of the CNRTL and say what each part commits the work to
questions.stem: A researcher consults the CNRTL, whose name expands into a phrase describing what the work sets out to do. What does the name promise?

options.text: A dictionary of national law, translated and revised, with every entry checked by a lawyer
options.misconception: believes the initials stand for a legal publishing house

options.text: A dictionary rationalised, updated and concerned with language as it is actually used across a wide period
A dictionary of regional languages, treated and reduced to the varieties spoken at the border
options.misconception: believes the name promises a dictionary of dialects only

options.text: A dictionary of technical terms, listed and ranked by the number of citations in the literature
options.misconception: believes the name promises a technical rather than a general dictionary

questions.explanation: The CNRTL stands for the Centre national de recherche des textes et du lexique, and the published dictionary that carries the initials expands into rationalised, updated, linguistic. Every word in that phrase is a commitment. Rationalised means the entries are regular rather than following whatever order the alphabet gave, so related words sit together. Updated means the work records changes that a printed page cannot show. Linguistic means the evidence is dated and attributed, so a reader can see whether a sense is eighteenth-century, nineteenth-century or recent, and whether it belongs to one writer or to general use. That is the difference from an alphabetical list, and it is why a researcher reaches for it first.
questions.hint: Ask what each of the three adjectives in the expanded name tells the reader to expect.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Two dated senses in one CNRTL dictionary entry
questions.learningObjective: read the two dated marks in a CNRTL entry and say what each one means
questions.stem: A dictionary entry prints a note under a word: the first use is marked with a date near 1800, and a second meaning is marked with a date near 1960. What do the two marks tell a reader?

options.text: That the first sense has died out and the second has replaced it entirely
options.misconception: believes a later date means an earlier sense has vanished

options.text: That the first sense is the older one and the second sense entered general use much later
That the second sense is a spelling mistake, since the word already had a meaning in 1800
options.misconception: reads a later sense as a mistake rather than as a later development

options.text: That the two dates mark the start and the end of one sense's period of use
options.misconception: reads a date printed under a sense as marking when that sense ended

questions.explanation: The dated marks under a CNRTL entry are evidence, not decoration. A date beside a sense says when that sense is first attested in the written record, so a sense marked near 1800 and a sense marked near 1960 tell the reader that the word acquired a second job about a century and a half later. A researcher can then ask which of the two a given text of 1850 could possibly be using, and that question cannot be answered by an undated entry at all. The marks also separate a general sense from one used by a single writer, which is a further distinction an alphabetical list does not carry.
questions.hint: Ask what a date placed under one sense and not another can be evidence of.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: A dated sense and a one-citation sense
questions.learningObjective: judge how much weight a single dated citation can carry in a lexicographic argument
questions.stem: A student argues that a sense of a word must be standard French because the dictionary records it. The entry gives exactly one dated citation from 1912. How should the student be answered?

options.text: A single dated citation shows the sense existed in 1912, but one citation is not enough to call the sense standard
A dictionary entry is definitive, so one citation is enough to settle the question for good
options.misconception: believes a dictionary carries a kind of authority no evidence can question

options.text: The sense cannot be dated at all, because lexicographers do not record when a sense appeared
options.misconception: believes lexicography cannot use dated evidence

options.text: The citation proves the sense was common in 1912, since a dictionary records only common usages
options.misconception: reads a single citation as evidence of common usage

questions.explanation: A dated citation is evidence that a sense was in use at the time of the text, and that is a real claim. It is not evidence that the sense was general, and the two are confused constantly. One citation establishes a lower bound, not a prevalence, and the whole apparatus of a scholarly dictionary exists to make that difference visible: attestations are gathered, dated, and grouped by author, and a sense resting on a single text is marked accordingly. So the student is partly right and partly wrong at once, and the useful response is not to dismiss the entry but to ask how many independent witnesses it has. One witness is a beginning, not a settlement.
questions.hint: Ask what the citation proves about 1912, and ask what it does not prove about the language.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: How a regional dictionary is built
questions.learningObjective: describe how a regional dictionary differs in scope from a national one
questions.stem: A regional dictionary documents the words of one area rather than the whole language. What does that choice of scope change?

options.text: It removes the need to date anything, since a single area is a single moment in time
options.misconception: believes a regional dictionary is exempt from dating evidence

options.text: It lets the editors record forms and senses that a national dictionary would leave out as too local
It makes the work easier, because a smaller area means fewer words to describe and to define
options.misconception: believes restricting the area reduces the work rather than redirecting it

options.text: It means the work can only be a dictionary of place names, since a region's identity is in its towns
options.misconception: believes regional vocabulary research is limited to toponyms

questions.explanation: A regional dictionary exists precisely to record what a national dictionary leaves out. Words used across a whole country, however few, are the business of a national dictionary; a local usage, a local name for a plant, a local verb for a trade, none of which travels, is the business of a regional one. That is not a lesser job but a different one, and it is often the only record of a form that has since died out. What does not change is the method: the same gathering of dated quotations, the same care about who said what, are needed before anyone can say what a region speaks.
questions.hint: Ask which words a national dictionary is obliged to leave out and a regional one is not.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The structure of a family of words around a shared root
questions.learningObjective: read a French word family as a single entry rather than as a list of separate words
questions.stem: A learner meets « peint, peintre, peinture, repeindre » in a dictionary, and the entries are grouped under one root. What does the grouping let the learner see?

options.text: That a single stem carries several parts of speech and several prefixes, each changing the sense in a fixed way
That the words share a spelling and nothing else, so the meanings must be learned one by one
options.misconception: believes a shared spelling carries no information about meaning

options.text: That all four words are adjectives, and that only the ending tells them apart
options.misconception: believes every member of the family is an adjective, as the participle ending suggests

options.text: That the group is dated, and that the oldest member in it is the one still used today
options.misconception: believes a word family is ordered by age with the oldest still current

questions.explanation: A family entry exists because the words in it are not independent. A single stem carries a participle, a noun, an agent noun and a verb, and the prefixes add a further layer with a regular job each: re- marks a second action, as in « repeindre ». Once that shape is visible the learner no longer memorises four meanings but one root and four predictable variations, and a new word built on the same stem can be understood before it is looked up. The grouping is not a stylistic convenience. It is the observation that these forms share a stem, and it is what makes a word family a better unit of learning than a word list.
questions.hint: Ask what the prefixes add to the stem, and what the endings add to it.

questions.stem: An international body for French-speaking states was created by a convention signed in the Nigerien capital in 1970. Which of these is the body it created?

options.text: the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation, created by a 1945 charter
options.misconception: confuses the Francophonie body with a general world organisation

options.text: the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie, whose membership reaches far beyond the countries of France
the African Union, whose predecessor was signed into being in the same Nigerian capital
options.misconception: confuses the Francophonie body with a continental union

options.text: the League of Nations, whose founding charter was signed at the same city and in the same year
options.misconception: confuses the body with an interwar organisation

questions.explanation: The convention of Niamey, signed in 1970, created what is now the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie, and the name of the city in which it was signed is the usual way of dating its foundation. It is a treaty organisation, not an agency of the United Nations, which is the distinction the second option tests.

questions.topic: What a francophonie counts and what it cannot count
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the ways of measuring the French-speaking world from one another
questions.stem: A researcher reports a single number for French speakers in the world and a critic objects. Which objection is the sound one?

options.text: The number depends on whether the researcher counted states, mother tongues, second languages, or daily users
The number is sound as long as it comes from a single census, since a census never miscounts
options.misconception: believes one official source makes a figure unarguable

options.text: The number is sound only if every speaker is counted, so a partial count is worthless
options.misconception: believes a partial count has no value whatever

options.text: The number is sound if it counts only those who write the language as well as speak it
options.misconception: believes literacy is the only defensible criterion for counting speakers

questions.explanation: There is no single agreed count of French speakers, and the reason is not that anyone is careless. The figure changes with the question asked: states where French is an official language count one way, people for whom French is a mother tongue count another, people who use it as a second language another, and daily users another again. In much of Africa the categories sit side by side, so a state may appear in one count and not another for perfectly good reasons. A researcher who states the category has made the figure usable; a researcher who states only the number has not, and the critic's objection is aimed at the second.
questions.hint: Ask which of four different populations the figure on the page was counting.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The official languages of Canada in law and in daily use
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a legal statement about official languages from a claim about daily use
questions.stem: A textbook says both English and French are the official languages of Canada, and a reader objects that the claim is misleading. What is the objection?

options.text: That official status applies only to the federal government and never to a province
options.misconception: believes official status cannot extend to a provincial level

options.text: That the constitution names only one official language, so the second was added by later statute
options.misconception: believes a single statute can override the constitutional text

options.text: That an official language is a legal status, and it says nothing on its own about how many people use it
That the two languages have equal status only in the capital and differ in every other region
options.misconception: believes legal equality holds in one place and not in others

questions.explanation: The distinction the reader is making is a real one and a useful habit to teach. Official language is a legal category: it says what a government may use in its own acts, what courts will accept, and what schools are required to provide. It does not measure how many people speak a language at home, and in Canada the two languages are close to mirror images in that respect, with English dominant outside Quebec and French dominant within it. So the legal statement is correct and a numerical claim built on top of it would be a separate claim needing separate evidence. A textbook that slides from one to the other has made an argument, not just an error.
questions.hint: Ask whether the clause is about what a government may do, or about what people do at home.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Keeping a language alive as a school subject
questions.learningObjective: explain what a school language keeps alive that a home does not
questions.stem: A reader notes that a language kept as a compulsory school subject can survive in a country where few families speak it at home. Why?

options.text: Because the school is the one setting that guarantees every child meets the language systematically, whatever the home does
Because a school subject is inherited by the next generation automatically, without anyone teaching it
options.misconception: believes a school subject transfers to families by itself

options.text: Because families that speak a language at home are not permitted to teach it to their children in school
options.misconception: believes a home language is excluded from the classroom

options.text: Because a compulsory school subject replaces the home entirely, so the two never have to overlap
options.misconception: believes a school language simply displaces whatever the home provides

questions.explanation: A language with no home base can still be kept alive by an institution, and the mechanism is straightforward: the school reaches every child, and a compulsory subject guarantees that none of them finishes without having met the language systematically. That is a guarantee a household cannot give, particularly in a minority position where most children arrive already speaking another language. What the school produces is not the same as a home language, and it is fair to say the two are not interchangeable. What the school can do is ensure that the next generation of teachers, writers and civil servants has the language at its disposal, which is what keeps the institutions themselves working.
questions.hint: Ask which institution can reach a child whose family does not speak the language at all.

options.misconception: believes the contest was restricted to schoolchildren

options.text: Designs from artists living in Europe, since the Acadian communities had not been consulted
options.misconception: believes the designs came from outside the Acadian communities

options.misconception: believes the flag came from one family's collection

questions.explanation: The Acadian flag was adopted in 1984, and it came out of a contest that ran for a year and collected submissions from Acadian communities on both sides of the Atlantic, in Canada and in the United States. questions.learningObjective: say what the general classification of a stage race measures
questions.stem: A stage race awards a jersey to the leader overall and a different colour to whoever leads a single stage. What does the overall classification measure?

options.text: The sum of the times over every stage, so a rider who is slow once can still lead the race
The time of the fastest single stage, so a rider who wins a stage leads the race
options.misconception: believes one good stage decides the general classification

options.text: The number of stages finished, so a rider who never drops out leads the race
options.misconception: believes the classification counts finishes rather than times

options.text: The result of the final stage alone, so everything before it is a warm-up
options.misconception: believes only the last stage counts towards the overall result

questions.explanation: The general classification is the sum of a rider's times over all the stages, and the lowest total wins. That is why a rider who wins a stage can still lose the race, and why a rider who loses time badly in one stage usually cannot make it up: the loss is added to the total just as the gains are. A bonus of seconds can be deducted for finishing high on a stage, which is why the totals in a results table are not simply the sum of the finishing times, and a reader who computes one from the other will find a discrepancy that is actually a rule.
questions.hint: Ask what is added up, and whether a single good stage can cancel a bad one.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The Tour de France, the Giro and the Vuelta
questions.learningObjective: name the three Grand Tours and the countries they are run in
questions.stem: A reader is told that three stage races make up the Grand Tour calendar. Which set of three is meant?

options.text: the Giro d'Italia, the Vuelta a España and the Tour de France, run in France, Italy and Spain
options.misconception: names the right three but attaches the countries in the wrong order

options.text: the Tour de France, the Giro d'Italia and the Vuelta a España, run in France, Italy and Spain
the Tour de France, the Vuelta a España and the Paris-Roubaix, run in France, Italy and Spain
options.misconception: substitutes a one-day race for one of the three stage races

options.text: the Tour de France, the Giro d'Italia and the Tour de Suisse, run in France, Italy and Spain
options.misconception: substitutes a different stage race for the one run in Spain

questions.explanation: The three Grand Tours are the Tour de France in France, the Giro d'Italia in Italy and the Vuelta a España in Spain, and all three run for about three weeks in the summer. The label is a modern invention rather than an official one, but it is the one a reader meets. The trap in the options is the third member, since the Vuelta is the race run in Spain and a reader who expects a French name in third place will substitute a Swiss or a Belgian one. What makes the three comparable is the length and the three-week window, not the country.
questions.hint: Ask which country each of the three races is run in, and check the third one carefully.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The Arianes and the launch site they use
questions.learningObjective: say which launch site the European Ariane rockets use
questions.stem: European satellites are launched by the Ariane rockets from one site. Which site is it?

options.text: Biarritz, in metropolitan France, where the site's latitude puts it close to the equator
options.misconception: names an unrelated Atlantic town as a launch site

options.text: Bourbon, in the Indian Ocean, where the site's latitude puts it close to the equator
options.misconception: confuses the space centre with a launch site in the Indian Ocean

options.text: Toulouse, in metropolitan France, where the site's latitude puts it close to the equator
options.misconception: names the town where the industrial office sits rather than the launch site

options.text: Kourou, in French Guiana, where the site's latitude puts it close to the equator

questions.explanation: Ariane launches from Kourou, in French Guiana, and the choice of site is a matter of physics rather than of politics: a rocket launched eastward gains speed from the rotation of the earth, and the gain is largest near the equator, so Kourou's latitude of about five degrees north is close to the best available on the planet. It also helps that the launch corridor opens over the Atlantic, so a launch that fails falls into ocean. The other options confuse the launch site with the administrative centre of the space programme or with an unrelated town.
questions.hint: Ask what a low latitude does for a rocket launched eastward, and which of the names is a real launch site.
